p: The Hebrew names Abijah's mother Micaiah. The Greek and Syriac call her Maacah, as Kings and 11:20 do.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("Michaiah"), ESV
readings.en: Micaiah daughter of Uriel from Gibeah

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); also the Syriac (as reported); NIV, NRSV ("Maacah")
readings.en: Maacah daughter of Uriel from Gibeon

why: The Plain keeps the Hebrew and explains the difference in a note. "Maacah" is probably the original name (1 Kings 15:2; 2 Chronicles 11:20; 15:16), but the Greek may have corrected the name to match those verses, so the evidence is not decisive.
b: The Greek also has "Gibeon" for "Gibeah," a common confusion between two Benjaminite towns. See the note on this verse for the family relationships.

p: The written Hebrew has Ephron; the Masoretes' reading note has Ephrain.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere); KJV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv); Septuagint (Brenton, checked); NIV, ESV, NRSV

why: The read form is the Masoretic reading tradition. Both forms probably name the same town, often identified with Ophrah of Benjamin (Joshua 18:23) and with the "Ephraim" near the wilderness to which Jesus withdrew (John 11:54), modern et-Taiyibeh.

a: in the Zephathah Valley at Mareshah
t: The valley of Zephathah, or north of Mareshah?
p: The Greek read the same Hebrew letters as "northward" (tsafonah) instead of a valley name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah
readings.plain: in the Zephathah Valley at Mareshah

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton; NRSV
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ φάραγγι κατὰ βορρᾶν Μαρισης
readings.en: in the valley north of Mareshah
readings.plain: in the valley north of Mareshah

why: The Hebrew gives a valley name known nowhere else. The Greek reading, "northward," differs by one letter and is accepted by many scholars. The Plain keeps the Hebrew; the sense is the same place either way.

a: the prophecy of Oded the prophet
t: Oded or Azariah son of Oded?
p: 15:1 names Azariah son of Oded, but here the Hebrew says "Oded the prophet." Some versions add "Azariah son of."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and the prophecy, Oded the prophet
readings.plain: the prophecy of Oded the prophet

readings.w: Syriac Peshitta and Latin Vulgate (as reported); BHS proposes the addition; NIV, ESV, NRSV
readings.en: and the prophecy of Azariah son of Oded the prophet
readings.plain: the prophecy of Azariah son of Oded the prophet

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer)
readings.en: the prophecy of Adad the prophet
readings.plain: the prophecy of Adad the prophet

why: The Hebrew is awkward: "the prophecy" has no "of" before "Oded," which suggests words dropped out. The Greek supports the shorter text, so the gap is old. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and notes that Azariah, Oded's son, is the speaker of 15:2–7.
b: Some think "Oded the prophet" was a note naming the father that crept into the text; others that a scribe skipped from one name to the next.

a: he took away the rank of queen mother from her, because she had made a horrid thing for Asherah
t: Queen mother, or priestess of Astarte?
p: The Greek says Asa removed Maacah from serving Astarte, the goddess, rather than from her rank.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); also 1 Kings 15:13
readings.en: he removed her from being queen mother, who had made for Asherah a horrid thing
readings.plain: he took away the rank of queen mother from her, because she had made a horrid thing for Asherah

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton
readings.orig: μετέστησεν τοῦ μὴ εἶναι τῇ Ἀστάρτῃ λειτουργοῦσαν
readings.en: he removed so that she should not serve Astarte
readings.plain: he removed from serving as priestess to Astarte

why: The Hebrew agrees with Kings. The Greek also lacks "crushed it" and calls the object simply "the idol." Its translator seems to have interpreted the rare words as describing pagan service, and replaced Asherah with the better-known Astarte. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew dates Baasha's attack to Asa's thirty-sixth year; the Greek has the thirty-eighth.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ὀγδόῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἔτει

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading and matches 15:19 (thirty-fifth year, no war). The Greek figure makes the chronology no easier. Neither fits Kings, where Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year; see the note on 15:19 for the explanations.

a: in the ways his forefather David had walked at first
p: The Greek lacks "David," so it refers to the early ways of Jehoshaphat's father Asa.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: in the first ways of David his father
readings.plain: in the ways his forefather David had walked at first

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); also some Hebrew manuscripts (as reported); NRSV
readings.orig: ἐν ὁδοῖς τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ ταῖς πρώταις
readings.en: in the first ways of his father
readings.plain: in the ways his father had walked at first

why: Most witnesses have "David," and Chronicles often compares kings with David (29:2; 34:2). The shorter Greek text fits the story of Asa's decline well, which may mean it is original, or that the translator saw the point and dropped a name that seemed odd. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

t: "They returned," or "to judge those in Jerusalem"?
p: The Hebrew ends oddly, "and they returned to Jerusalem." The Greek has "and to judge those who live in Jerusalem."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("when they returned to Jerusalem")
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Latin Vulgate similar (as reported); NRSV
readings.orig: καὶ κρίνειν τοὺς κατοικοῦντας ἐν Ιερουσαλημ
readings.en: and to judge those living in Jerusalem
readings.plain: They were also to judge the people living in Jerusalem.

readings.w: The same Hebrew letters read with other vowels (a repointing proposed by scholars); NIV ("And they lived in Jerusalem"), ESV ("They had their seat at Jerusalem")
readings.en: and they sat (or dwelt) in Jerusalem
readings.plain: They had their seat in Jerusalem.

why: The Hebrew is kept, though it is hard: it may mean the king and his officials returned to Jerusalem after the tour of 19:4, or that the court sat in Jerusalem. The Greek reflects Hebrew letters read as "the inhabitants of Jerusalem" (yoshve), which many scholars accept. A third option keeps the letters but reads wayyeshevu, "they sat" (as a court) or "they lived," which is what the NIV and ESV translate.

p: The Hebrew says "some of the Ammonites," after Ammonites were already named. The Greek has the Meunites (Minaeans).

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer) ("Minaeans"); NIV, ESV, NRSV
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("beside the Ammonites")

why: Here the Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew repeats "the Ammonites" just named, which makes no sense, and the two words differ only by the order and shape of a few letters (me'ammonim / me'unim). The Meunites appear with the Arabs in 26:7 and in 1 Chronicles 4:41, and 20:10 and 20:22–23 speak of a third group, "Mount Seir," which fits a people from Edom's region.
b: The Meunites were probably named after Ma'an, a town southeast of Petra, in Edomite territory. The Greek calls them Minaeans, the name of a well-known Arabian people.

p: The Hebrew says the army came "from Aram." One Hebrew manuscript and most modern versions read "from Edom."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer) ("from Syria"); KJV
One medieval Hebrew manuscript (as reported); NIV, ESV, NRSV

why: Aram (Syria) lay far to the north, and an army coming around the Dead Sea to En-gedi came from Edom, the land of "Mount Seir" (20:10). In Hebrew script, d and r look nearly alike, so "Edom" and "Aram" were often confused (as in 2 Samuel 8:12–13). "Edom" is almost certainly the sense. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and Greek, since both read Aram.

a: goods, dead bodies, and costly things
p: The Hebrew lists "dead bodies" among the plunder. A few Hebrew manuscripts and the Latin read "clothing."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("dead bodies")
readings.en: and goods and corpses and precious things
readings.plain: goods, dead bodies, and costly things

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate ("vestes"), as reported; NIV, ESV, NRSV
readings.en: and goods and garments and precious things

why: "Dead bodies" in a list of plunder is strange, but it can be read as saying the goods were found on and among the bodies. "Clothing" (begadim) differs by one letter from "corpses" (pegarim) and fits the list better, so many scholars and translations prefer it. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.
b: The Greek (Brenton, checked) lists livestock, baggage, spoils and precious things, without bodies or clothing.

t: King of Israel or of Judah?
p: The Hebrew calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel." The Greek and other versions say "king of Judah."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Syriac, Latin Vulgate and some Hebrew manuscripts (as reported); CSB, NRSV

why: "Judah" is the expected title and may be a correction. Chronicles often uses "Israel" for Judah as the true heir of all Israel (12:6; 21:4; 23:2), so "king of Israel" may be the Chronicler's own phrase. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew says Jehoram built high places on Judah's mountains; the Greek says in Judah's towns.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Latin Vulgate (as reported)

why: The two Hebrew words, be-hare (mountains) and be-'are (towns), differ by one letter. High places on hills make good sense, and Kings speaks of high places "in all the towns of Judah" elsewhere (2 Kings 23:5), which could explain a change in either direction. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew calls the youngest son Jehoahaz; the Greek calls him Ahaziah, as 22:1 does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); NIV ("Ahaziah")

why: The two names have the same parts in reverse order (see the note), and the Hebrew uses both for one man. The Greek has made the names uniform. The Plain keeps the Hebrew form, as the site does with all royal names.

p: The Hebrew makes Ahaziah forty-two at his accession, older than his father, who died at forty. Kings says twenty-two.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NKJV, ASV, JPS 1917
2 Kings 8:26; Lucianic Greek and Syriac (as reported, not checked); ESV (footnote "forty-two"), NIV, NASB, CSB, NRSV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton

why: Forty-two cannot be right: Jehoram became king at thirty-two and reigned eight years (21:20), so a son of forty-two would have been born before his father. Twenty-two (Kings) is almost certainly correct, and forty-two is best explained as a copying slip, perhaps from a number written as a letter (mem, forty, for kaf, twenty) or from the forty-two relatives of 2 Kings 10:14. The Plain keeps the Masoretic figure, as the KJV and NKJV do, so that the reader sees the problem.
b: Some harmonizers tried to save the figure by counting forty-two years from the founding of Omri's dynasty (Athaliah was Omri's granddaughter), an explanation found in medieval Jewish commentators such as Radak. This is not the natural sense of the formula.

p: The Hebrew spells "the Arameans" without its first letter, so it can be read "the archers." The Greek took it that way.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (read with 2 Kings 8:28 as "the Arameans"); KJV ("the Syrians"), NIV, ESV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton

why: Kings has "the Arameans" with the full spelling, and the Hebrew here is probably a shortened spelling of the same word. "Archers" (from ramah, "to shoot") is a possible reading of the letters, and Joram was wounded in battle with Aram either way.

p: The Hebrew here calls the king of Judah "Azariah." Kings, the Greek and several versions have Ahaziah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); some Hebrew manuscripts, Syriac and Latin Vulgate (as reported); 2 Kings 8:29; NIV, ESV, NRSV

why: "Azariah" is almost certainly a copying slip for "Ahaziah": the names share most letters, and the whole passage is about Ahaziah. But it is the Masoretic text, and the site's policy is not to change a king's name silently, so the Plain keeps "Azariah" and gives Ahaziah here. Readers should understand the same king as in 22:1–9.
b: The same verse also has "because the wounds" where Kings has "from the wounds"; the Plain translates by the sense, as Kings has it.

p: The Hebrew says Jehu killed "the sons of Ahaziah's brothers." The Greek says "Ahaziah's brothers," as Kings does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: and the sons of the brothers of Ahaziah

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton; compare 2 Kings 10:13

why: The Hebrew fits Chronicles' own story, in which Ahaziah's brothers had already been killed (21:17). The Greek may have conformed to Kings. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

t: Hiding or being treated for his wounds?
p: The Hebrew has Ahaziah hiding in Samaria; the Greek has him being treated for his wounds there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV
readings.en: and he was hiding in Samaria

readings.w: Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton
readings.en: they caught him being healed in Samaria

why: The Greek reflects mitrappe, "being healed," which differs from mitchabbe, "hiding," by two letters and echoes "to be healed" in 22:6 and in 2 Kings 9:15–16. It would make Ahaziah a wounded king under treatment, closer to Kings (2 Kings 9:27), rather than a fugitive. It may be a correction toward 22:6 or the original. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew names the priest's son Zechariah. The main Greek manuscripts call him Azariah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all English versions
Septuagint, Rahlfs edition (based mainly on Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus; checked by this writer); Brenton

why: The Hebrew is followed. The Greek may have confused him with one of the many Azariahs of this period (21:2; 22:6; 23:1). Jesus' saying about "the blood of Zechariah" (Luke 11:51; Matthew 23:35) presupposes the name Zechariah.

a: the sons of Jehoiada the priest
p: The Hebrew says "the blood of the sons of Jehoiada." The Greek and Latin have "the son," meaning Zechariah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.plain: the sons of Jehoiada the priest

readings.w: Septuagint as translated by Brenton (1844, from the Vaticanus-based Sixtine text; checked by this writer) (Greek text not checked directly); Latin Vulgate (as reported); NIV, ESV, NRSV
readings.plain: the son of Jehoiada the priest

why: The story tells of one son's murder, so the singular is the natural sense, and many scholars think the plural is a slip or a "plural of category." Some take the plural at face value: Joash may have killed other sons of Jehoiada too. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: His sons, the great oracle against him
t: "The great oracle" or "may the oracle be great"?
p: Written Hebrew: "the greatness of the burden"; read form: "may the burden be great." The Greek differs again.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written form (Ketiv); KJV ("the greatness of the burdens")
readings.en: and the greatness of the burden
readings.plain: His sons, the great oracle against him

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read form (Qere)
readings.plain: His sons (may the oracle against him be great)

readings.w: Septuagint as translated by Brenton (1844, from the Vaticanus-based Sixtine text; checked by this writer) (Greek text not checked directly)
readings.en: and the five came to him
readings.plain: His sons, and the five who came to him

why: Here the Plain follows the written form, which gives the clearer sense in a list of topics, and keeps its singular; many translations make it plural ("the many oracles"). The read form makes the words a wish or curse. The Greek apparently read different letters (perhaps chamishah, "five").
b: On the meaning of massa, "burden" or "oracle," see the note.
